lesson.title: The Equals Sign That Isn't Equality: How Assignment Works
lesson.summary: Assignment is the operation that binds a name to a value, and understanding that Python always evaluates the right side completely before touching the name on the left explains behavior that otherwise looks like a mathematical contradiction.
lesson.body:
In Python, the single equals sign, =, is the assignment operator, and it is important to separate it firmly from mathematical equality, which in Python is written as a double equals sign, ==. When you write name = expression, you are not claiming that name equals expression the way an equation does. You are giving an instruction: first fully evaluate whatever is on the right side of the equals sign to produce a value, and only after that value is ready, bind the name on the left side to it. This order of operations, right side first, then left side, is not just a technical detail, it is the reason a statement like x = x + 1 makes complete sense in code even though it would be a contradiction as a mathematical equation.

Python also supports a few variations on basic assignment. Chained assignment lets you write a = b = 5, which binds both a and b to the value 5 in one statement. Simultaneous assignment lets you write a, b = 1, 2, which binds a to 1 and b to 2 at the same time, evaluating the entire right side before any binding happens, which is why a, b = b, a is a common, reliable way to swap two variables' values in Python without needing a temporary variable.

The right-side-first rule is easiest to see by tracing a slightly longer example carefully:

x = 5
y = x
x = x + 1
print(x, y)

Line one binds x to the integer object 5. Line two evaluates the right side, x, which means looking up what x currently refers to, 5, and binds y to that same value, 5. It is critical to see that y is bound to the value 5 itself at that moment, not somehow linked to x forever, so y will not automatically change just because x changes later. Line three evaluates its right side first: look up x, which is 5, add 1, producing 6, and only then does the name x get rebound to this new value, 6. The name y was never touched by this line. So print(x, y) outputs 6 5, showing x updated to 6 while y stayed at 5, because y captured x's value at the time of assignment rather than tracking x going forward.

This behavior, that assignment copies a value at a specific moment rather than creating a permanent link between two names, is one of the most common sources of confusion for beginners, who sometimes expect y to change whenever x changes later. It helps to remember that the right side of an assignment is always fully resolved into a concrete value before the left side is touched at all, so by the time y = x actually binds y, Python has already finished looking up x and has a plain value, 5, in hand, with no ongoing relationship to the name x left behind.

Keeping the two rules straight, evaluate the right side completely first, and assignment captures a value at that instant rather than an ongoing connection, will explain the behavior of nearly every assignment statement you write from here on, including more advanced patterns you will meet later where a variable is reassigned repeatedly inside a loop, one evaluation at a time, each one building on whatever value the name most recently held.
